title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 388
paragraphs: In this way he won the Egyptians to himself, so that they consented to be his subjects. His ordering of affairs was as follows. In the early morning and until the time when the marketplace filled, he willingly conducted whatever business was brought before him, but after that he spent his time drinking and jesting with his boon-companions, behaving frivolously and playfully. His friends, troubled by this, admonished him in words such as these: “O king, you are not governing yourself rightly by descending to such trifling behavior. You ought rather to be sitting the whole day in dignity on a dignified throne and conducting your business; and so the Egyptians would know for certain that they were ruled by a great man, and you would have a better reputation. As it is, you are behaving in no way like a king.” And he answered them thus: “Those who have bows string them when they wish to use them, and when they have finished using them they unstring them again; for if they were always kept strung, they would break, so that the men could not use them when they had need. So too is the state of a man: if he were always in earnest and did not relax himself for sport at the proper time, he would either go mad or become struck with stupor before he was aware of it; and knowing this well, I give a portion of my time to each of the two ways of living.” Such was his answer to his friends.
